semantically_equivalent_domains.justification: Partial monitoring typically involves dealing with systems or environments where complete information is not available at all times, closely aligning with the concept of partially observable environments.
Partial monitoring often relates to decision-making processes in environments with partial observability, similar to the scenarios addressed by partially observable Markov decision processes.

parent_domains.justification: Partial monitoring may often involve detecting deviations from expected patterns or behaviors, associating it with broader anomaly detection techniques.
Partial monitoring can involve tracking changes in the observed system or environment, connecting it to the broader concept of change detection.

closest_parent_domain.justification: Change detection is the most direct parent domain for partial monitoring, as both involve observing and responding to changes in limited or partially observed contexts.

child_domains.justification: This domain can be considered a specification under partial monitoring, since it addresses decision making in environments where monitoring is partial.

closest_child_domain.justification: Among child domains, the focus on decision processes under partial observability makes this the closest to partial monitoring.

sibling_domains.justification: Both partial monitoring and anomaly detection involve identifying inconsistencies or unexpected variations, sharing the same closest parent domain of change detection.
Bayesian change point detection is closely related to monitoring changes, similar to partial monitoring, under the parent domain of change detection.
Time-series anomaly detection shares the observational and detection goals of partial monitoring under the common parent of change detection.
This domain involves detecting instances that deviate from the trained model's distribution, similar in concept to how partial monitoring would handle unexpected changes.

closest_sibling_domain.justification: Within the siblings identified under change detection, anomaly detection is the most direct parallel to the concept of monitoring for unexpected variations or anomalies.

unrelated_domains.justification: Health monitoring is domain-specific and not directly related to partial observability or change detection.
Similar to health monitoring, this domain is applied to a specific area not directly linked to partial monitoring in a theoretical context.
Action state tracking involves more continuous monitoring rather than dealing with partial observability.
Fire monitoring is a specific application area and doesn't align with the general theory of partial observability.
While related to monitoring, unobtrusive sensing focuses more on the method of data collection rather than the challenges of partial data.
This is a field-specific application and not theoretically related to partial observability or change detection concepts.
Similar to unobtrusive sensing, automated sensing focuses more on the means of collection rather than the theoretical aspects of partial data.
Software analytics involves data analysis specific to software development, differing from the theoretical focus of partial monitoring.
System analysis tends to be more structured and comprehensive than the inherently uncertain nature of partial monitoring.
This domain is more specific to software and not related to partial observability challenges.
While it involves monitoring, diagnostics are more about identifying faults rather than dealing with partial or incomplete information.
Data auditing is concerned with the accuracy and completeness of data post-collection, unlike the focus on dealing with partial data in real-time.
Object tracking usually involves full or near-full information about the objects, unlike partial monitoring scenarios.
